Decomposition numbers for weight 3 3 blocks of Iwahori–Hecke algebras of type B B
Matthew Fayers Lorenzo Putignano Queen Mary University of London Università degli Studi di Firenze m.fayers@qmul.ac.uk lorenzo.putignano@unifi.it

Abstract
Let B B be a weight- 3 3 block of an Iwahori–Hecke algebra of type B B over any field. We develop the combinatorics of B B to prove that the decomposition numbers for B B are all 0 0 or 1 1 .



2020 Mathematics subject classification: 20C08, 20C30, 05E10

1
Introduction

In the representation theory of the symmetric groups, a fundamental problem is to determine the
decomposition numbers
in characteristic
p
: the composition multiplicities of
p
-modular simple representations in
p
-modular reductions of ordinary simple representations. A complete solution to this problem seems far out of reach, but solutions are known in various special cases. One of these results (due to the first author
[
F4
]
) says that the decomposition numbers in a
p
-block of weight
3
in characteristic
p\geqslant 5
are all either
0
or
1
; this in particular allows these decomposition numbers to be computed quickly using the Jantzen–Schaper formula.

The decomposition number problem naturally extends to the Iwahori–Hecke algebras of type
A
, where we seek the composition multiplicities of the simple modules in the Specht modules. Many of the known results for symmetric groups have been proved for the Iwahori–Hecke algebras as well, including the result for blocks of weight
3
. More recently, this problem has been extended to the Iwahori–Hecke algebras
\mathcal{H}_{n}
of type
B
. These were first systematically studied by Dipper, James and Murphy
[
DJM
]
, who introduced appropriate definitions of Specht modules labelled by bipartitions of
n
. This naturally leads to a combinatorial approach to the corresponding decomposition number problem, underpinned by the combinatorics of bipartitions. The first author’s combinatorial definition of the weight of a bipartition, and hence the weight of a block
[
F1
]
, allows us to approach this problem systematically by addressing blocks of a fixed weight. As in type
A
, the blocks of weight
0
are precisely the simple blocks, and blocks of weight
1
admit a very simple description (analogous to symmetric group blocks with cyclic defect groups). The first author
[
F2
]
gave a combinatorial formula for decomposition number for blocks of weight
2
, analogous to Richards’s formula
[
R
]
for type
A
.

In this paper we address blocks of weight
3
. Our main result is as follows.

Theorem 1.1
.

Suppose
\mathbb{F}
is a field,
q\in\mathbb{F}
is non-zero, and
k_{1},k_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}
. Let
\mathcal{H}_{n}
denote the Iwahori–Hecke algebra of type
B
over
\mathbb{F}
with parameters
q,q^{k_{1}},q^{k_{2}}
, and let
B
be a block of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
of weight
3
. Then the decomposition numbers for
B
are all either
0
or
1
.

Note in particular that (unlike in type
A
)
1.1
applies even when
\mathbb{F}
has characteristic
2
or
3
. We conjecture that this result extends to all weight
3
blocks of
Ariki–Koike algebras
; these are higher-level Hecke algebras generalising the Iwahori–Hecke algebras of types
A
and
B
. A particular case of this conjecture (the case of ‘tree blocks’) has already been proved by Lyle and Ruff in
[
LR
]
.

The proof of
1.1
is by induction on
n
, using the Brundan–Kleshchev branching rules which govern induction and restriction between
\mathcal{H}_{n}
and
\mathcal{H}_{m}
, for
m<n
. An important part of our work is a combinatorial description of all the bipartitions labelling Specht modules in a given block, and an analysis of which Specht modules
\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
cannot be shown to be multiplicity-free via the inductive hypothesis. For the most difficult cases, we need to use the cyclotomic Jantzen–Schaper formula due to James and Mathas
[
JM1
]
.

Acknowledgements
.

Most this work was developed while the second author was visiting Queen Mary University of London between October 2022 and April 2023. The second author expresses his sincere gratitude to the University of Florence for having funded the visit and to the first author and the whole QMUL maths department for their hearty hospitality.

2
Background

In this section we summarise some of the background results we shall need. For notation we mostly follow the first author’s paper
[
F2
]
, where more details and motivation may be found.

2.1
Basic notation

In this paper
\mathbb{N}
denotes the set of positive integers. Throughout, we fix an integer
e\geqslant 2
. For any integer
a
, we write
\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{a}=a+e\mathbb{Z}=\left\{\left.a+em\ \right|\ \smash{m\in\mathbb{Z}}\right\}
, and
\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}=\left\{\left.\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{a}\ \right|\ \smash{a\in\mathbb{Z}}\right\}
. The set
\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
admits an additive action of
\mathbb{Z}
via
a+\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{b}=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{a}
.

In general, given any tuple
\left\{\left.x_{i}\ \right|\ \smash{i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}}\right\}
of objects indexed by
\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
, and given an integer
a
, we may write
x_{a}
to mean
x_{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{a}}
. Similarly, given any terminology involving an element of
\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
(such as ‘
i
-node’), we may substitute an integer
a
in place of
\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{a}
(so we may define an
a
-node to mean an
\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{a}
-node).

Throughout the paper, we fix a pair
\kappa=(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2})\in(\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z})^{2}
. A pair of integers
k_{1},k_{2}
such that
\kappa_{1}=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{k}
and
\kappa_{2}=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{k}
is called a
bicharge
for
\kappa
.

If
M
and
N
are modules for an algebra, then we write
M\sim N
to mean that
M
and
N
have the same composition factors with multiplicity.

2.2
Partitions and bipartitions

A
partition
is an infinite weakly-decreasing sequence
\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\dots)
of integers which are eventually zero. We write
\lvert\lambda\rvert
for the sum
\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\dots
, and say that
\lambda
is a partition of
\lvert\lambda\rvert
. When writing partitions, we omit trailing zeroes and group together equal parts with a superscript. We write
\varnothing
for the unique partition of
0
. For any partition
\lambda
, we write
h(\lambda)
for the number of non-zero parts of
\lambda
, which we call the
length
of
\lambda
.

A
bipartition
is an ordered pair
\lambda=\big(\lambda^{(1)}\ \big|\ \lambda^{(2)}\big)
of partitions, which we call the
components
of
\lambda
. We write
\lvert\lambda\rvert=\lvert\lambda^{(1)}\rvert+\lvert\lambda^{(2)}\rvert
, and say that
\lambda
is a bipartition of
\lvert\lambda\rvert
.

The Young diagram of a bipartition
\lambda
is the set

[\lambda]=\left\{\left.(r,c,a)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\times\{1,2\}\ \right|\ \smash{c\leqslant\lambda^{(a)}_{r}}\right\},

whose elements we call the
nodes
of
\lambda
. In general, a node means an element of
\mathbb{N}^{2}\times\{1,2\}
. A node
(r,c,a)
of
\lambda
is
removable
if it can be removed from
[\lambda]
to leave the Young diagram of a smaller bipartition (that is, if
c=\lambda^{(a)}_{r}>\lambda^{(a)}_{r+1}
), while a node not in
\lambda
is an addable node of
\lambda
if it can be added to
[\lambda]
to leave a Young diagram.

We depict
[\lambda]
by drawing the Young diagram of
\lambda^{(1)}
above the Young diagram of
\lambda^{(2)}
(using the English convention). Accordingly, we will say that a node
(r,c,a)
is
above
or
higher than
a node
(s,d,b)
if either
a<b
or
a=b
and
r<s
.

If
\lambda
and
\mu
are two bipartitions of
n
, then we say that
\lambda

dominates

\mu
(and write
\lambda\trianglerighteqslant\mu
) if

\lambda^{(1)}_{1}+\dots+\lambda^{(1)}_{r}\geqslant\mu^{(1)}_{1}+\dots+\mu^{(1)}_{r}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lvert\lambda^{(1)}\rvert+\lambda^{(2)}_{1}+\dots+\lambda^{(2)}_{r}\geqslant\lvert\mu^{(1)}\rvert+\mu^{(2)}_{1}+\dots+\mu^{(2)}_{r}

for every
r\geqslant 1
. Another way of saying this is that
[\mu]
can be obtained from
[\lambda]
by moving one or more nodes to lower positions.

If
\lambda
is a partition, the
conjugate
partition
\lambda^{\prime}
is defined by

(\lambda^{\prime})_{r}=\lvert\left\{\left.c\in\mathbb{N}\ \right|\ \smash{\lambda_{c}\geqslant r}\right\}\rvert.

If
\lambda
is a bipartition, the conjugate bipartition is
\lambda^{\prime}=\big({\lambda^{(2)}}^{\prime}\ \big|\ {\lambda^{(1)}}^{\prime}\big)
. In other words,
\lambda^{\prime}
is obtained by interchanging the two components, and then replacing each component with the conjugate partition. Note then that if
\lambda,\mu
are two bipartitions, then
\lambda\trianglerighteqslant\mu
if and only if
\mu^{\prime}\trianglerighteqslant\lambda^{\prime}
.

Now suppose we have fixed a pair
\kappa=(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2})\in(\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z})^{2}
. The
residue
of a node
(r,c,a)
, denoted
\operatorname{res}(r,c,a)
, is
c-r+\kappa_{a}
. If
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
, then an
i
-node
means a node of residue
i
. If
\lambda
is a bipartition, then the
content
of
\lambda
is the multiset of the residues of the nodes of
\lambda
. For any
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
, we write
\operatorname{rem}_{i}(\lambda)
for the number of removable
i
-nodes of
\lambda
.

We will also need to consider rim hooks. The
rim
of a bipartition
\lambda
is the set of nodes
(r,c,a)\in[\lambda]
such that
(r+1,c+1,a)\notin[\lambda]
. A
rim hook
of
\lambda
is a connected subset of the rim which can be removed to leave a smaller bipartition. If
H
is a rim hook, the
hand node

\operatorname{hand}(H)
is the top-rightmost node of
H
, and the
leg length

\operatorname{ll}(H)
is the difference in height between the highest and lowest nodes in
H
.

2.3
Beta-sets and the abacus

We often use James’s abacus for partition combinatorics. With
e
fixed as above, we take an abacus with
e
vertical runners labelled
0,\dots,e-1
from left to right, and with positions marked
0,1,\dots
from left to right along successive rows of the abacus, working down the page. Now given a partition
\lambda
and an integer
k\geqslant h(\lambda)
, we define the
beta-set for
\lambda
with charge
k
to be the set
\left\{\left.\lambda_{r}+k-r\ \right|\ \smash{1\leqslant r\leqslant k}\right\}
. The
abacus display
for
\lambda
with charge
k
is constructed by placing a bead on the abacus at position
\lambda_{r}+k-r
for each
1\leqslant r\leqslant k
.

Given a bipartition
\lambda=\big(\lambda^{(1)}\ \big|\ \lambda^{(2)}\big)
and a bicharge
(k_{1},k_{2})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}
with
k_{a}\geqslant h(\lambda^{(a)})
for
a=1,2
, the abacus display for
\lambda
with bicharge
(k_{1},k_{2})
is obtained by placing the abacus display for
\lambda^{(1)}
with charge
k_{1}
above the abacus display for
\lambda^{(2)}
with charge
k_{2}
.

The abacus is good for visualising rim hooks (and in particular, removable nodes). Given an abacus display for a bipartition
\lambda
, removable nodes in component
a
correspond to positions
x>0
on the abacus such that in component
a
there is a bead at position
x
but no bead at position
x-1
. Given such a
x
, the residue of the corresponding removable node is
x+e\mathbb{Z}
. Similarly, addable nodes correspond to positions
x
such that there is a bead at position
x-1
but not at position
x
.

More generally, rim hooks in component
a
of
\lambda
correspond to pairs of positions
x,y
where
x>y
and there is a bead at position
x
but not at position
y
in component
a
. The residue of the hand node of the corresponding rim hook is
x+e\mathbb{Z}
, the leg length is the number of beads between positions
x
and
y
(not including position
x
), and removing the rim hook corresponds to moving the bead at position
x
to position
y
.

2.4
Restricted bipartitions

In
[
AM
]
, Ariki and Mathas introduced a set of multipartitions to provide a combinatorial labelling for simple modules of Ariki–Koike algebras. They called these
Kleshchev multipartitions
, but here we prefer the term
restricted multipartitions
introduced by Brundan–Kleshchev
[
BK
]
. We now recall the definition here, specialising to the case of bipartitions. We will use the original recursive definition of Ariki–Mathas, though we note that a more efficient definition was found by Ariki, Kreiman and Tsuchioka
[
AKT
]
.

The definition of restricted bipartitions depends on our fixed
\kappa\in(\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z})^{2}
. Take a bipartition
\lambda
and a residue
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
. Define the
i
-signature
of
\lambda
to be the sequence of signs obtained by reading the Young diagram of
\lambda
from top to bottom, writing
+
for each addable
i
-node and
-
for each removable
i
-node. The
reduced
i
-signature
is the subsequence obtained by repeatedly deleting adjacent pairs
-+
. The removable nodes corresponding to the
-
signs are called the
normal

i
-nodes of
\lambda
, and the highest of these (if there are any) is the
good

i
-node. The addable nodes corresponding to the
+
signs in the reduced
i
-signature are the
conormal

i
-nodes of
\lambda
, and the lowest of these (if there are any) is the
cogood

i
-node.

For any bipartition
\mu
and any
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
, we write
\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)
for the number of normal
i
-nodes of
\mu
.

Example
.

Suppose
e=3
,
\kappa=(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{},\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{})
and
\lambda=\big(3,2,1^{2}\ \big|\ 2^{3}\big)
. The Young diagram of
\lambda
is shown below, with the residues of the addable and removable nodes indicated.

\vphantom{1}\smash{2}
\vphantom{1}\smash{0}
\vphantom{1}\smash{0}
\vphantom{1}\smash{1}
\vphantom{1}\smash{2}
\vphantom{1}\smash{0}
\vphantom{1}\smash{2}
\vphantom{1}\smash{0}
\vphantom{1}\smash{0}
\vphantom{1}\smash{1}

If we let
i=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}
, then we see that the
i
-signature of
\lambda
is
+--+-
. So the reduced
i
-signature is
+--
. So there are two normal
i
-nodes
(2,2,1)
and
(3,2,2)
, with
(2,2,1)
being the good
i
-node. There is a unique conormal (and therefore cogood)
i
-node
(1,4,1)
.

Now given two bipartitions
\lambda
and
\mu
, write
\mu\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\longrightarrow}}\lambda
if
\mu
is obtained from
\lambda
by removing the good
i
-node for
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
, or equivalently if
\lambda
is obtained from
\mu
by adding the cogood
i
-node. We write
\mu\longrightarrow\lambda
to mean that
\mu\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\longrightarrow}}\lambda
for some
i
, and let
\longleftrightarrow
be the equivalence relation generated by
\longrightarrow
. Now define the set of restricted bipartitions (with respect to
\kappa
) to be the bipartitions in the
\longleftrightarrow
-class containing
\big(\varnothing\ \big|\ \varnothing\big)
.

The definition of restricted bipartitions derives from the theory of crystals for highest-weight representations of quantum groups. It follows from this theory (in particular, the uniqueness of highest-weight vectors) that the only restricted bipartition with no normal nodes of any residue is
\big(\varnothing\ \big|\ \varnothing\big)
. So to test whether a bipartition
\lambda
is restricted, one can repeatedly remove arbitrarily-chosen good nodes until there are no good nodes remaining; then
\lambda
is restricted if and only if the resulting bipartition is
\big(\varnothing\ \big|\ \varnothing\big)
.

We also make an observation which will be helpful later on. Say that a partition
\lambda
is
e
-restricted
if
\lambda_{r}-\lambda_{r+1}<e
for all
r
. Now the following is a well-known result; it reflects that restricted bipartitions label the vertices of a level-
2
highest-weight crystal obtained as a component of the tensor product of two level-
1
crystals, which themselves have vertices labelled by
e
-restricted partitions.

Lemma 2.1
.

Suppose
\lambda
is a restricted bipartition. Then both
\lambda^{(1)}
and
\lambda^{(2)}
are
e
-restricted partitions.

It is an easy exercise to check that if
\lambda,\mu
are bipartitions with
\mu\longrightarrow\lambda
, and
a\in\{1,2\}
, then
\lambda^{(a)}
is
e
-restricted if and only if
\mu^{(a)}
is. Since the components of the empty bipartition
\big(\varnothing\ \big|\ \varnothing\big)
are both
e
-restricted, the result follows.
∎

We will also need to consider
regular
bipartitions. These are described in
[
F2
, 1.3.3]
, where they are called
conjugate Kleshchev
bipartitions. We say that a bipartition
\lambda
is
regular
if
\lambda^{\prime}
is restricted. In fact we can modify the above definition of restricted bipartitions to give an alternative description of regular bipartitions, which will be useful later. To do this, define the
i
-signature of a bipartition as above, and define the
antireduced

i
-signature by successively deleting pairs
+-
. The removable nodes corresponding to
-
signs in the antireduced
i
-signature are called the
antinormal

i
-nodes of
\lambda
, and the lowest of these (if there are any) is the
antigood

i
-node. Similarly, the addable nodes corresponding to
+
signs are the
anticonormal

i
-nodes of
\lambda
, and the highest of these (if there are any) is the
anticogood

i
-node. Given two bipartitions
\lambda
and
\mu
, we write
\mu\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\Longrightarrow}}\lambda
if
\mu
is obtained from
\lambda
by removing the antigood
i
-node for some
i
. Equivalently, if we write
i^{\prime}=\kappa_{1}+\kappa_{2}-i
, then
\mu\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\Longrightarrow}}\lambda
if and only if
\mu^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i^{\prime}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\lambda^{\prime}
. Now let
\Longrightarrow
be the union of the relations
\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\Longrightarrow}}
, and let
\Longleftrightarrow
be the equivalence relation generated by
\Longrightarrow
. The bipartitions in the
\Longleftrightarrow
-class containing
\big(\varnothing\ \big|\ \varnothing\big)
are the regular bipartitions.

2.5
Iwahori–Hecke algebras

We fix a field
\mathbb{F}
with
q,Q_{1},Q_{2}
non-zero elements of
\mathbb{F}
, and let
\mathcal{H}_{n}
denote the Iwahori–Hecke algebra of type
B
with parameters
q,Q_{1},Q_{2}
. This is the unital associative
\mathbb{F}
-algebra with generators
T_{0},\dots,T_{n-1}
, subject to relations

\displaystyle(T_{0}-Q_{1})(T_{0}-Q_{2})

\displaystyle=0,

\displaystyle(T_{i}-q)(T_{i}+1)

\displaystyle=0

\displaystyle\text{for }1\leqslant i<n,

\displaystyle T_{i}T_{j}

\displaystyle=T_{j}T_{i}

\displaystyle\text{if }j-i>1,

\displaystyle T_{0}T_{1}T_{0}T_{1}

\displaystyle=T_{1}T_{0}T_{1}T_{0},

\displaystyle T_{i}T_{i+1}T_{i}

\displaystyle=T_{i+1}T_{i}T_{i+1}

\displaystyle\text{for }1\leqslant i<n-1.

The definition of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
is unaffected if we interchange
Q_{1}
and
Q_{2}
, but it will be important for us to consider
(Q_{1},Q_{2})
as an ordered pair; in particular, the construction of Specht modules depends on this ordered pair. (In
Section

2.7
below, we consider in more detail the effect of interchanging
Q_{1}
and
Q_{2}
.)

As explained in
[
F2
, 1.3.2]
, using a Morita equivalence result of Dipper–James
[
DJ
]
, we can restrict attention to the case where
Q_{1}
and
Q_{2}
are powers of
q
. We also assume that
q
is a primitive
e
th root of unity, where
e\geqslant 2
; the case where
q
is not a root of unity works in the same way as the case where
e>n
(and in fact most of the particular cases of blocks that we consider only arise if
q
is an
e
th root of unity for
e\leqslant n
).

So with our fixed pair
\kappa=(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}^{2}
, we will assume henceforth that
Q_{1}=q^{k_{1}}
and
Q_{2}=q^{k_{2}}
, where
(k_{1},k_{2})
is any bicharge for
\kappa
.

The representation theory of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
is based on the theory of
Specht modules
. For each bipartition
\lambda
of
n
, we write
\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
for the corresponding Specht module, as defined in Mathas’s survey article
[
M2
]
. The Specht modules are precisely the cell modules with respect to a particular cellular basis of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
, and a central problem in the representation theory of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
is to determine their composition factors. To do this, we need a classification of the simple
\mathcal{H}_{n}
-modules. If
\lambda
is a restricted bipartition, then
\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
has a unique simple quotient
\operatorname{D}_{\lambda}
, and the simple modules
\operatorname{D}_{\lambda}
arising in this way give a complete irredundant set of simple
\mathcal{H}_{n}
-modules. Thus the problem of determining the composition factors of the Specht modules amounts to determining the
decomposition numbers

[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
, where
\lambda,\mu
are bipartitions of
n
with
\mu
restricted.

A fundamental result on decomposition numbers is the following.

Proposition 2.2

(
[
F2
, Theorem 1.2]
)
.

If
\lambda
and
\mu
are bipartitions of
n
with
\mu
restricted, then
[\operatorname{S}_{\mu}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=1
, while if
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]>0
then
\lambda\trianglerighteqslant\mu
.

2.6
Blocks and weight

An important tool for studying the decomposition number problem is the classification of blocks, since
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=0
unless
\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
and
\operatorname{D}_{\mu}
lie in the same block. It is a consequence of the general theory of cellular algebras that a Specht module always belongs to a single block, and we will abuse notation by saying that
\lambda
lies in a block
B
to mean that
\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
lies in
B
. Of course, if
\lambda
is restricted this means that
\operatorname{D}_{\lambda}
lies in this block too, so to classify the blocks of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
it is sufficient to determine when two Specht modules lie in the same block. The block classification for
\mathcal{H}_{n}
is a special case of the result for Ariki–Koike algebras proved by Lyle and Mathas.

Proposition 2.3

(
[
LM
, Theorem 2.11]
)
.

Suppose
\lambda
and
\mu
are bipartitions of
n
. Then
\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
and
\operatorname{S}_{\mu}
lie in the same block of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
if and only if
\lambda
and
\mu
have the same content.

As explained in
[
F1
, 3.2]
, this result can also be formulated in terms of the abacus: if we choose a bicharge
(k_{1},k_{2})
for
\kappa
with
k_{1},k_{2}
sufficiently large, and construct the abacus displays for
\lambda
and
\mu
with this bicharge, then
\lambda
and
\mu
have the same content if and only if for each
i
the number of beads on runner
i
(across both components) is the same in each abacus display. This leads to another useful way to determine whether two bipartitions belong to the same block. If
\lambda
is a bipartition, then for each
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
we define
\delta_{i}(\lambda)
to be the number of removable
i
-nodes of
\lambda
minus the number of addable
i
-nodes of
\lambda
. Now we have the following result.

Proposition 2.4

(
[
F1
, Proposition 3.2]
)
.

Suppose
\lambda
and
\mu
are bipartitions of
n
. Then
\lambda
and
\mu
lie in the same block if and only if
\delta_{i}(\lambda)=\delta_{i}(\mu)
for all
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
.

As a consequence we can define
\delta_{i}(B)
for a block
B
, meaning
\delta_{i}(\lambda)
for any bipartition
\lambda
in
B
. If
a\in\mathbb{Z}
, then we may write
\delta_{a}(B)
to mean
\delta_{a+e\mathbb{Z}}(B)
.

In
[
F1
]
, the first author introduced the notion of the
weight

\operatorname{wt}(\lambda)
of a bipartition
\lambda
. Since the weight of
\lambda
depends only on the content of
\lambda
, it is the same for all
\lambda
in a given block, and therefore one may define the weight of a block
B
to be the weight of any bipartition in
B
. The weight of
B
is a non-negative integer which measures the complexity of
B
, and a fruitful approach to the representation theory of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
is to consider blocks of a given small weight.

We will not give the definition of weight in terms of content here, but we will use the results from
[
F2
, 1.3.5]
showing how to calculate the weight of a bipartition using the abacus. We will introduce the necessary notation in
Section

3
.

We will also use the following lemma several times.

Lemma 2.5

(
[
F1
, Lemma 3.6]
)
.

Suppose
\lambda
is a bipartition, and that
\mu
is a bipartition obtained by removing
u
removable
i
-nodes from
\lambda
. Then

\operatorname{wt}(\mu)=\operatorname{wt}(\lambda)+u(\delta_{i}(\lambda)-u).

This paper is motivated by the following result.

Theorem 2.6
.

Suppose
B
is a block of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
of weight
0
,
1
or
2
, and
\lambda,\mu
are bipartitions in
B
with
\mu
restricted. Then
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]\leqslant 1
.

The result for blocks of weight
0
follows from
[
F1
, Theorem 4.1]
, and the result for weight
1
is
[
F1
, Theorem 4.2]
. For blocks of weight
2
, the result is given in
[
F2
, Theorems 3.18 & 4.13]
.
∎

Our aim in this paper is to prove the same result for blocks of weight
3
. In fact for blocks of weight at most
2
explicit formulæ for the decomposition numbers are known; for weight
3
we just show that the decomposition numbers are at most
1
(which is enough to enable the decomposition numbers to be computed quickly using the Jantzen–Schaper formula). This is analogous to the situation for Hecke algebras of type
A

[
F4
]
.

2.7
Conjugation and component-switching

The set of bipartitions of
n
has very natural symmetries, given by conjugation or by simply interchanging components. These symmetries provide useful tools for studying decomposition numbers, which we describe here.

We begin with conjugation, which relates to automorphisms. Let
\theta
be the automorphism defined defined by mapping
T_{0}\mapsto q^{k_{1}+k_{2}}T_{0}^{-1}
and
T_{i}\mapsto-qT_{i}^{-1}
for
i\geqslant 1
. For any
\mathcal{H}_{n}
-module
M
, define the module
M^{\theta}
by twisting the
\mathcal{H}_{n}
-action by
\theta
. Obviously if
M
is simple then so is
M^{\theta}
, and so we can define a bijection
\mu\mapsto\mu^{\diamond}
from the set of restricted bipartitions to the set of regular bipartitions by
(\operatorname{D}_{\mu})^{\theta}\cong\operatorname{D}_{(\mu^{\diamond})^{\prime}}
. Understanding what the automorphism
\theta
does to Specht modules gives us more information on decomposition numbers, as follows.

Proposition 2.7
.

Suppose
\lambda
and
\mu
are bipartitions of
n
with
\mu
restricted. Then
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda^{\prime}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{(\mu^{\diamond})^{\prime}}]
.

Our argument is based on
[
M1
, Sections 4 and 5]
, where Mathas recalls the
dual Specht module

\operatorname{S}^{\prime}(\lambda)
for each
\lambda
. The dual Specht modules are related to the usual Specht modules in two ways. On the one hand, one can check that
\operatorname{S}^{\prime}(\lambda)
is isomorphic to
(\operatorname{S}_{\lambda})^{\theta}
. To see this, we recall how
\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
is constructed: a certain element
m_{\lambda}\in\mathcal{H}_{n}
is defined, and
\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
is defined to be the right ideal generated by
m_{\lambda}
, modulo its intersection with the two-sided ideal generated by the elements
m_{\nu}
for
\nu\vartriangleright\lambda
. The dual Specht module
\operatorname{S}^{\prime}(\lambda)
is defined similarly using a different element
n_{\lambda}
. But one can check that
\theta(m_{\lambda})
equals
n_{\lambda}
times an invertible element of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
, so that the (right or two-sided) ideal generated by
\theta(m_{\lambda})
coincides with the (right or two-sided) ideal generated by
n_{\lambda}
. As a consequence, we obtain
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=[\operatorname{S}^{\prime}(\lambda):(\operatorname{D}_{\mu})^{\theta}]
for all
\lambda,\mu
.

On the other hand, Mathas considers contragredient duality
M\mapsto M^{\circledast}
induced by the antiautomorphism of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
that fixes each
T_{i}
. In
[
M1
, Corollary 5.7]
Mathas shows that
\operatorname{S}^{\prime}(\lambda)\cong(\operatorname{S}_{\lambda^{\prime}})^{\circledast}
. Since contragredient duality preserves composition multiplicities, and the simple modules are self-dual (which follows from the cellularity of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
), we find that
[\operatorname{S}^{\prime}(\lambda):\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda^{\prime}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
for every
\lambda,\mu
. The result follows.
∎

Corollary 2.8
.

Suppose
\lambda
and
\mu
are bipartitions of
n
, with
\mu
restricted. Then
[\operatorname{S}_{\mu^{\diamond}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=1
, while if
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]>0
then
\mu^{\diamond}\trianglerighteqslant\lambda
.

This follows from
2.2
and
2.7
using the fact that conjugation reverses the dominance order on bipartitions.
∎

Later in the paper we will need to be able to calculate the bijection
⋄
combinatorially. Recall the relations
\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\longrightarrow}}
and
\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\Longrightarrow}}
from
Section

2.4
.

Proposition 2.9
.

Suppose
\lambda
and
\mu
are restricted bipartitions. Then
\mu\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\longrightarrow}}\lambda
if and only if
\mu^{\diamond}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\Longrightarrow}}\lambda^{\diamond}
.

The Brundan–Kleshchev modular branching rules show that the relation
\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\longrightarrow}}
can be described algebraically via

\mu\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\longrightarrow}}\lambda\qquad\text{if and only if }\qquad\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{H}_{n-1}}(\operatorname{D}_{\mu},\mathrm{e}_{i}\operatorname{D}_{\lambda})\neq 0,

where
\mathrm{e}_{i}
is the
i
th restriction functor (see
Section

2.8
below). The definition of
\mathrm{e}_{i}
and the automorphism
\theta
shows that
(\mathrm{e}_{i}M)^{\theta}=\mathrm{e}_{i^{\prime}}(M^{\theta})
for any module
M
, where as above
i^{\prime}=\kappa_{1}+\kappa_{2}-i
. Hence

\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{H}_{n-1}}(\operatorname{D}_{\mu},\mathrm{e}_{i}\operatorname{D}_{\lambda})\neq 0\qquad\text{if and only if }\qquad\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{H}_{n-1}}(\operatorname{D}_{(\mu^{\diamond})^{\prime}},\mathrm{e}_{i^{\prime}}\operatorname{D}_{(\lambda^{\diamond})^{\prime}})\neq 0,

and therefore

\mu\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\longrightarrow}}\lambda\qquad\text{if and only if }\qquad(\mu^{\diamond})^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i^{\prime}}}{{\longrightarrow}}(\lambda^{\diamond})^{\prime},

and from
Section

2.4
this is equivalent to
\mu^{\diamond}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\Longrightarrow}}\lambda^{\diamond}
.
∎

Now we come to component-switching, where we don’t need to say as much. If
\lambda
is a bipartition, let
\lambda^{\leftrightarrow}
denote the bipartition
\big(\lambda^{(2)}\ \big|\ \lambda^{(1)}\big)
obtained by switching the two components of
\lambda
. Note that although the isomorphism type of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
only requires the unordered pair
(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2})
, the definition of the Specht module (and the associated combinatorics of residues, blocks, restricted bipartitions etc) depends on the ordered pair
(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2})
. We let
{\operatorname{S}}^{\leftrightarrow}_{\lambda}
denote the Specht module constructed using the bipartition
\lambda^{\leftrightarrow}
and the ordered pair
(\kappa_{2},\kappa_{1})
.

Lemma 2.10
.

Suppose
\lambda
is a bipartition of
n
. Then
\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
and
{\operatorname{S}}^{\leftrightarrow}_{\lambda}
have the same composition factors (with multiplicity).

This uses a specialisation argument. Let
\hat{q},\hat{Q}_{1},\hat{Q}_{2}
be algebraically independent indeterminates over
\mathbb{F}
, and consider the Iwahori–Hecke algebra
\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{n}
over
\mathbb{F}(\hat{q},\hat{Q}_{1},\hat{Q}_{2})
with parameters
\hat{q},\hat{Q}_{1},\hat{Q}_{2}
. Then
\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{n}
is semisimple by
[
A
, Main Theorem]
, with the Specht modules being the simple modules. If we define the Specht module
\hat{\operatorname{S}}_{\lambda}
for
\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{n}
using the bipartition
\lambda
and the parameters
\hat{q},\hat{Q}_{1},\hat{Q}_{2}
, and we define the Specht module
\hat{\operatorname{S}}^{\leftrightarrow}_{\lambda}
using the bipartition
\lambda^{\leftrightarrow}
and the parameters
\hat{q},\hat{Q}_{2},\hat{Q}_{1}
, then a consideration of characters shows that
\hat{\operatorname{S}}_{\lambda}
and
\hat{\operatorname{S}}^{\leftrightarrow}_{\lambda}
are isomorphic. The
\mathcal{H}_{n}
-modules
\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
and
{\operatorname{S}}^{\leftrightarrow}_{\lambda}
are obtained by specialising
\hat{q}
to
q
,
\hat{Q}_{1}
to
q^{k_{1}}
and
\hat{Q}_{2}
to
q^{k_{2}}
, where
\kappa_{1}=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{k}
,
\kappa_{2}=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{k}
. It is a standard result on specialisation that specialisations of isomorphic modules have the same composition factors.
∎

Lemma

2.10
allows us to reduce the work we do in considering different types of blocks: given a block
B
of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
, we can study the same block by replacing
\kappa
with
(\kappa_{2},\kappa_{1})
and replacing each bipartition
\lambda
in
B
with
\lambda^{\leftrightarrow}
. The truth of
1.1
for
B
is then independent of which way we view
B
.

2.8
Branching rules

Now we summarise some essential background on the Brundan–Kleshchev branching rules; the most comprehensive reference for these is
[
BK
]
. Recall that the content of a bipartition is the multiset of the residues of its nodes, and that two bipartitions lie in the same block if and only if they have the same content. So we may define the content
\mathcal{C}_{B}
of a block
B
to be the content of any bipartition in
B
.

Now suppose
M
is an
\mathcal{H}_{n}
-module lying in a block
B
, and
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
. If there is a block
A
of
\mathcal{H}_{n-1}
such that
\mathcal{C}_{A}
is obtained by removing a copy of
i
from
\mathcal{C}_{B}
, then we define
\mathrm{e}_{i}M
to be the block component of
M\downarrow_{\mathcal{H}_{n-1}}
lying in
A
; otherwise, we set
\mathrm{e}_{i}M=0
.

The functors
\mathrm{e}_{i}
are defined for all
n
, so we can define powers
\mathrm{e}_{i}^{r}
. In fact, it is possible to define
divided powers
: for any
\mathcal{H}_{n}
-module
M
and for any
r
there is an
\mathcal{H}_{n-r}
-module
\mathrm{e}_{i}^{(r)}M
such that
\mathrm{e}_{i}^{r}M\cong(\mathrm{e}_{i}^{(r)}M)^{\oplus r!}
. For any non-zero module
M
, we set
\epsilon_{i}M=\max\left\{\left.r\ \right|\ \smash{\mathrm{e}_{i}^{r}M\neq 0}\right\}
.

The following results are essential tools in the study of decomposition numbers. Recall that we write
\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)
for the number of normal
i
-nodes of a bipartition
\mu
and
\operatorname{rem}_{i}(\lambda)
for the number of removable
i
-nodes of
\lambda
.

Proposition 2.11
.

1.

Suppose
\lambda
is a bipartition of
n
. Then
\mathrm{e}_{i}^{(r)}\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
has a filtration in which the factors are the Specht modules
\operatorname{S}_{\nu}
, for all bipartitions
\nu
that can be obtained from
\lambda
by removing
r
removable
i
-nodes. In particular,
\epsilon_{i}\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}=\operatorname{rem}_{i}(\lambda)
, and
\mathrm{e}_{i}^{(\epsilon_{i}\operatorname{S}_{\lambda})}\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
is isomorphic to the Specht module
\operatorname{S}_{\lambda^{-}}
, where
\lambda
is the bipartition obtained by removing all the removable
i
-nodes from
\lambda
.

2.

Suppose
\mu
is a restricted bipartition of
n
. Then
\epsilon_{i}\operatorname{D}_{\mu}=\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)
and
\mathrm{e}_{i}^{(\epsilon_{i}\operatorname{D}_{\mu})}\operatorname{D}_{\mu}\cong\operatorname{D}_{\mu^{-}}
, where
\mu^{-}
is the bipartition obtained by removing all the normal
i
-nodes from
\mu
.

2.9
The cyclotomic Jantzen–Schaper formula

The cyclotomic Jantzen–Schaper formula introduced by James and Mathas
[
JM1
]
will be a very useful tool. We describe a special case here, specialising to the case of Hecke algebras of type
B
.

First we note that because every field is a splitting field for
\mathcal{H}_{n}
, we can extend the field
\mathbb{F}
without affecting the representation theory. So we assume that the subfield of
\mathbb{F}
generated by
q
is a proper subfield, and we fix an element
x
of
\mathbb{F}
lying outside this subfield.

Let
\hat{q}
be an indeterminate over
\mathbb{F}
, and let
R=\mathbb{F}[\hat{q}^{\pm 1}]
. Choose a bicharge
(k_{1},k_{2})
for
\kappa
for which
|k_{1}-k_{2}|>n
. Let
\mathfrak{p}
be the prime ideal in
R
generated by
\hat{q}-q
. We want to consider the Iwahori–Hecke algebra of type
B
over
R
with parameters
\hat{q},\hat{Q}_{1},\hat{Q}_{2}
, where

\hat{Q}_{1}=\hat{q}^{k_{1}},\qquad\hat{Q}_{2}=\hat{q}^{k_{2}}+x(\hat{q}-q).

Now given a node
(r,c,a)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\times\{1,2\}
define

\widehat{\operatorname{res}}(r,c,a)=\hat{q}^{c-r}\hat{Q}_{a}\in R.

Now suppose
\lambda
and
\nu
are bipartitions of
n
with
\lambda\vartriangleright\nu
. Let
G(\lambda,\nu)
be the set of all pairs
(L,N)
such that

\diamond

L
is a rim hook of
\lambda
and
N
a rim hook of
\nu
,

\diamond

[\lambda]\setminus L=[\nu]\setminus N
, and

\diamond

\operatorname{res}(\operatorname{hand}(L))=\operatorname{res}(\operatorname{hand}(N))
.

Given a pair
(L,N)\in G(\lambda,\nu)
, define
\epsilon_{LN}=(-1)^{\operatorname{ll}(L)-\operatorname{ll}(N)}
, and let

j_{\lambda\nu}=\prod_{(L,N)\in G(\lambda,\nu)}\big(\widehat{\operatorname{res}}(\operatorname{hand}(L))-\widehat{\operatorname{res}}(\operatorname{hand}(N))\big)^{\epsilon_{LN}}.

Now for any pair of bipartitions
(\lambda,\mu)
with
\mu
restricted, we define

J_{\lambda\mu}=\sum_{\nu\vartriangleleft\lambda}\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}(j_{\lambda\nu})[\operatorname{S}_{\nu}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}].

The following statement is a special case of the Jantzen–Schaper formula
[
JM1
, Theorem 4.6]
.

Theorem 2.12

(
[
JM1
, Theorem 4.6]
)
.

Suppose
\lambda
and
\mu
are bipartitions of
n
with
\mu
restricted. Then the decomposition number
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
is at most
J_{\lambda\mu}
, and is non-zero if and only if
J_{\lambda\mu}
is non-zero.

Our particular choice of
\hat{q},\hat{Q}_{1},\hat{Q}_{2}
means that the values
\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}(j_{\lambda\nu})
will be easy to compute, and will not depend on the characteristic of
\mathbb{F}
for the cases we will need to consider. In particular, suppose
(r,c,a)
and
(s,d,b)
are nodes. Then it is easy to check that:

\diamond

if
a\neq b
, then

\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}(\widehat{\operatorname{res}}(r,c,a)-\widehat{\operatorname{res}}(s,d,b))=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\operatorname{res}(r,c,a)=\operatorname{res}(s,d,b),\\
0&\text{otherwise};\end{cases}

\diamond

if
a=b
, then

\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}(\widehat{\operatorname{res}}(r,c,a)-\widehat{\operatorname{res}}(s,d,b))=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }c-r=d-s\pm e,\\
0&\text{if }c-r\not\equiv d-s\ (\operatorname{mod}\,e).\end{cases}

We can use the Jantzen–Schaper formula to refine
2.2
and
2.8
, by using a coarser order than the dominance order. We write
\lambda\blacktriangleright\nu
if
\lambda\vartriangleright\nu
and
\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}(j_{\lambda\nu})\neq 0
, and we extend
\blacktriangleright
reflexively and transitively to give a partial order, which we call the
Jantzen–Schaper dominance
order; note that this order depends on our fixed parameters
e
and
\kappa
. It is easy to see that the usual dominance order is a refinement of the Jantzen–Schaper dominance order, and that conjugation of bipartitions reverses the Jantzen–Schaper dominance order. Moreover,
2.12
allows us to strengthen
2.2
and
2.8
.

Proposition 2.13
.

Suppose
\lambda
and
\mu
are bipartitions with
\mu
restricted and
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]>0
, then
\mu^{\diamond}\trianglerighteqslant\lambda\trianglerighteqslant\mu
in the Jantzen–Schaper dominance order.

The fact that
\lambda\trianglerighteqslant\mu
is immediate from
2.12
. This then implies that
\mu^{\diamond}\trianglerighteqslant\lambda
, using
2.7
and the fact that the Jantzen–Schaper dominance order is reversed by conjugation.
∎

With this result in mind, we will use the Jantzen–Schaper order from now on, so we will write
\trianglerighteqslant
for the Jantzen–Schaper order. Although this order is harder to work with, it will help us to narrow down the cases we need to consider. Note that when trying to decide whether
\lambda\trianglerighteqslant\mu
in the Jantzen–Schaper order, the usual dominance order can be used as a “first pass”: if
\lambda\ntrianglerighteqslant\mu
in the usual dominance order, then certainly
\lambda\ntrianglerighteqslant\mu
in the Jantzen–Schaper order. To examine the Jantzen–Schaper order more closely, it will be helpful to be able to visualise it on the abacus. Take two bipartitions
\lambda,\nu
, and take the abacus displays for these bipartitions. In order to obtain
\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}(j_{\lambda\nu})\neq 0
, we need to be able to get from the abacus display for
\lambda
to the abacus display for
\nu
by moving a bead from position
b_{1}
to position
c_{1}
on component
i_{1}
, and a bead from position
c_{2}
to position
b_{2}
on component
i_{2}
, where
i_{1},i_{2}\in\{1,2\}
,
b_{1}-c_{1}=b_{2}-c_{2}>0
, and
b_{1}\equiv b_{2}\ (\operatorname{mod}\,e)
. We then have
\lambda\vartriangleright\nu
if and only if either
b_{1}>b_{2}
or
i_{1}<i_{2}
. The leg length of the hook
L
removed from
\lambda
is the number of beads between positions
b_{1}
and
c_{1}
, and the leg length of the hook removed from
\nu
is the number of beads between positions
b_{2}
and
c_{2}
.

For example, take
e=6
,
\kappa=(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{},\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{})
,
\lambda=\big(2\ \big|\ 4,2,1^{2}\big)
and
\nu=\big(2,1^{4}\ \big|\ 4\big)
. Taking the bicharge
(11,10)
, we obtain the following abacus displays. (We draw the beads that have moved in white.)

\begin{array}[]{c@{\qquad}c}\lambda&\nu\\[5.0pt]

Taking
b_{1}=b_{2}=10
,
c_{1}=c_{2}=6
,
i_{1}=1
and
i_{2}=2
, we see that
j_{\lambda\nu}\neq 0
and
\lambda\vartriangleleft\nu
. Alternatively, we can see this by looking at the Young diagrams (in which we label nodes with their residues, and shade the involved rim hooks).

3
Blocks of weight
3

3.1
Weight and the abacus

In this section we summarise results from
[
F1
]
showing how to calculate the weight of a bipartition from the abacus, and then use these to describe bipartitions of weight
3
.

Suppose
\lambda
is a bipartition, and construct the abacus display for
\lambda
using the bicharge
(k_{1},k_{2})
. We compute the weight of
\lambda
recursively, in three stages.

First suppose there is a bead in the abacus display with an unoccupied position immediately above. Define a new abacus display (and hence a new bipartition
\lambda^{-}
) by moving the bead up into this empty space (this corresponds to removing a rim
e
-hook from
\lambda
). Then
[
F1
, Corollary 3.4]
gives
\operatorname{wt}(\lambda^{-})=\operatorname{wt}(\lambda)-2
.

Applying this repeatedly, we can assume that
\lambda
is a
bicore
; that is, it has no rim
e
-hooks. Now for each
x\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
define
\gamma_{x}(\lambda)
to equal the number of beads on runner
x
in component
1
minus the number of beads on runner
x
in component
2
of the abacus display. (Note that
\gamma_{x}(\lambda)
depends on the choice of bicharge
(k_{1},k_{2})
, but the difference
\gamma_{x}(\lambda)-\gamma_{y}(\lambda)
for
x,y\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
does not.) Now for
x,y\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
with
x\neq y
define the bicore
s_{xy}(\lambda)
by moving a bead from component
1
to component
2
on runner
x
, and a bead from component
2
to component
1
on runner
y
of the abacus display. Then
[
F1
, Lemma 3.7]
shows that
\operatorname{wt}(s_{xy}(\lambda))=\operatorname{wt}(\lambda)-2(\gamma_{x}(\lambda)-\gamma_{y}(\lambda)-2)
.

This shows that whenever there are
x,y
with
\gamma_{x}(\lambda)-\gamma_{y}(\lambda)\geqslant 3
, we can replace
\lambda
with a bipartition
s_{xy}(\lambda)
of smaller weight. By doing this repeatedly (and using the fact that weight is always non-negative) we can reduce to the case where
\lambda
is a bicore with
\gamma_{x}(\lambda)-\gamma_{y}(\lambda)\leqslant 2
for all
x,y\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
. In this case we use
[
F1
, Proposition 3.8]
, which gives
\operatorname{wt}(\lambda)=\min\{\lvert X\rvert,\lvert Y\rvert\}
, where

\displaystyle X

\displaystyle=\left\{\left.x\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}\ \right|\ \smash{\gamma_{x}(\lambda)-\gamma_{y}(\lambda)=2\text{ for some }y\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}}\right\},

\displaystyle Y

\displaystyle=\left\{\left.y\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}\ \right|\ \smash{\gamma_{x}(\lambda)-\gamma_{y}(\lambda)=2\text{ for some }x\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}}\right\}.

In particular, we note that
\operatorname{wt}(\lambda)=0
if and only if
\lambda
is a bicore with
\gamma_{x}(\lambda)-\gamma_{y}(\lambda)\leqslant 1
for all
x,y\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
.

Example
.

Suppose
e=5
,
(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2})=(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{},\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{})
and
(k_{1},k_{2})=(9,9)
, and let
\lambda
be the bipartition
\big(5,3\ \big|\ 6,4,3\big)
, with the following abacus display.

\begin{array}[]{c}\hbox to60.64pt{\vbox to36.4pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\enskip\lower-32.41444pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}}{}
{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}}{}}{}
{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}}{}}{}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 -1.75 L 0 5.24 L 10.49 5.24}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}}{}
{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}}{}}{}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}}{}}{{}}{}
{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}}{}}{}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 17.48 -1.75 L 17.48 5.24 M 6.99 5.24 L 27.97 5.24}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

Then
\operatorname{wt}(\lambda)=\operatorname{wt}(\lambda^{-})+4
and
\operatorname{wt}(\lambda^{-})=\operatorname{wt}(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{})+2
, since
\gamma_{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}}(\lambda^{-})-\gamma_{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}}(\lambda^{-})=3
. Now
\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}
satisfies
\gamma_{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}}(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{})-\gamma_{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}}(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{})=2
and
\gamma_{x}(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{})-\gamma_{y}(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{})\leqslant 1
for all other
x,y\in\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}
. In the above notation we have that
|X|=|Y|=1
which implies
\operatorname{wt}(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{})=1
. We conclude that
\operatorname{wt}(\lambda)=7
.

We can use these results to describe blocks of weight
3
; this is very similar to the description of blocks of weight
2
in
[
F2
, Section 2.1]
. The above results show that if
\lambda
is a bipartition in a block
B
of weight
3
, then one of the following occurs.

1a.

\lambda
has a rim
e
-hook, and removing this leaves a bipartition of weight
1
.

1b.

\lambda
is a bicore, and there are
x,y\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
such that
\gamma_{x}(\lambda)-\gamma_{y}(\lambda)=3
and
s_{xy}(\lambda)
has weight
1
.

2.

\lambda
is a bicore with
\gamma_{i}(\lambda)-\gamma_{j}(\lambda)\leqslant 2
for all
i,j
, and
\min\{\lvert X\rvert,\lvert Y\rvert\}=3
, where
X
and
Y
are as defined above.

We observe that if
\lambda^{-}
is obtained by removing a rim
e
-hook from
\lambda
, then
\delta_{i}(\lambda^{-})=\delta_{i}(\lambda)
for all
i
, because
\delta_{i}(\lambda)
is determined by the total number of beads on each runner (across both components) in the abacus display for
\lambda
, which does not change when we move a bead up its runner. Similarly, if
\lambda
is a bicore then
\delta_{i}(s_{xy}(\lambda))=\delta_{i}(\lambda)
for all
i
. In view of
[
F1
, Lemma 3.3]
, we then obtain
\lvert s_{xy}(\lambda)\rvert=n-e
. So in cases (1a) and (1b) there is a block
A
of some
\mathcal{H}_{n-e}
with weight
1
and with
\delta_{i}(A)=\delta_{i}(B)
for all
i
.

If
B
contains a bipartition satisfying (2) above, then (following
[
F3
]
) we say that
B
is a
core block
. By
[
F3
, Theorem 3.1]
, this is equivalent to the statement that there is no block
A
of
\mathcal{H}_{m}
for any
m
with weight less than
3
, and with
\delta_{i}(A)=\delta_{i}(B)
for all
i
.

What this means is that if
B
is a core block of weight
3
then the bipartitions in
B
all satisfy (2), while if
B
is a non-core block then the bipartitions in
B
all satisfy (1a) or (1b).

In
Section

3.3
we will see that our main theorem is easy to prove for core blocks, but we need to consider non-core blocks in detail.

3.2
The bipartitions in a non-core weight
3
block

Suppose
B
is a non-core block of weight
3
. In this section we show how to construct all the bipartitions in
B
. Suppose
\lambda
is a bipartition in
B
, and take an abacus display for
\lambda
with bicharge
(k_{1},k_{2})
. Then we can construct a bipartition
\nu
lying in a block
A
of weight
1
with
\delta_{i}(\nu)=\delta_{i}(\lambda)
for all
i
(either by removing a rim
e
-hook or by applying
s_{xy}
for some
x,y
). We call
A
the
weight
1
block underlying
B
. Now
\gamma_{x}(\nu)-\gamma_{y}(\nu)\leqslant 2
for all
x
and
y
, and if we define the sets
X
and
Y
as in
Section

3
(with
\nu
in place of
\lambda
), then
\min\{\lvert X\rvert,\lvert Y\rvert\}=1
. We will assume that
\lvert Y\rvert=1
, with the other case being similar. We set
Z=X\cup Y
and
\mathcal{C}(Z)=\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}\setminus Z
; note in particular that
|Z|\geqslant 2
. Now define a new abacus display (with bicharge
(k_{1}+1,k_{2}-1)
) by moving a bead from component
2
to component
1
on runner
y
(where
Y=\{y\}
). We denote the resulting bipartition
\xi_{A}
, and call it the
nucleus
of
A
. Then
\xi_{A}
is independent of the choice of
\nu
(and hence independent of the choice of
\lambda
), and the
(\kappa_{1}+1,\kappa_{2}-1)
-weight of
\xi_{A}
is
0
. Moreover, if we define the integers
\gamma_{x}(\xi_{A})
using the abacus display with bicharge
(k_{1}+1,k_{2}-1)
, then

\gamma_{x}(\xi_{A})-\gamma_{y}(\xi_{A})=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }x\in Z,\ y\in\mathcal{C}(Z)\\
-1&\text{if }x\in\mathcal{C}(Z),\ y\in Z\\
0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Now for each for each
z\in Z
define a bipartition
\nu_{z}
in
A
by taking the abacus display for
\xi_{A}
and moving a bead from component
1
to component
2
on runner
z
. Then the description of the bipartitions in a weight
1
block in
[
F1
, Section 4.2.1]
shows that the bipartitions
\nu_{z}
for
z\in X\cup Y
are precisely the bipartitions in
A
. Now the results in
Section

3
show that each bipartition in
B
is obtained from a bipartition
\nu_{z}
in
A
either by adding a rim
e
-hook or by applying the operator
s_{xy}
for some
x,y
for which
\gamma_{x}(\nu_{z})-\gamma_{y}(\nu_{z})=1
. But the above formula for
\gamma_{x}(\xi_{A})-\gamma_{y}(\xi_{A})
shows that
\gamma_{x}(\nu_{z})-\gamma_{y}(\nu_{z})=1
if and only if either
x\in Z\setminus\{z\}
and
y\in\mathcal{C}(Z)
, or
x\in\mathcal{C}(Z)
and
y=z
.

This enables us to describe (and label) all the bipartitions in
B
. These come in three families, constructed from
\xi_{A}
as follows.

\diamond

For each
z\in Z
,
x\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
and
a\in\{1,2\}
, we obtain a bipartition
\operatorname{a}_{x}^{(a)}{}{\downarrow}^{z}
from
\xi_{A}
by moving a bead from component
1
to component
2
on runner
z
, then moving the lowest bead on runner
x
on component
a
down one position.

\diamond

For each
x\in\mathcal{C}(Z)
, we obtain a bipartition
\downarrow^{x}
from
\xi_{A}
by moving a bead from component
1
to component
2
on runner
x
.

\diamond

For each
w,z\in Z
with
w\neq z
and for each
y\in\mathcal{C}(Z)
, we obtain a bipartition
\downarrow^{w,z}\uparrow_{y}
from
\xi_{A}
by moving beads from component
1
to component
2
on runners
w
and
z
, and then moving a bead from component
2
to component
1
on runner
y
.

Example
.

Suppose
e=4
,
(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2})=(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{},\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{})
and
(k_{1},k_{2})=(8,7)
. Let
B
be the weight-
3
block of
\mathcal{H}_{10}
containing the bipartition
\lambda=\big(4\ \big|\ 4,1^{2}\big)
. Then the underlying weight-
1
block
A
comprises the bipartitions
\big(3,1^{3}\ \big|\ \varnothing\big)
,
\big(3\ \big|\ 1^{3}\big)
and
\big(\varnothing\ \big|\ 4,1^{2}\big)
, and the nucleus of
A
is
\xi_{A}=\big(2\ \big|\ 1^{2}\big)

We see that
Z=\{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{},\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{},\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}\}
. So there are
28
bipartitions in
B
: the bipartitions
\operatorname{a}_{x}^{(a)}{}{\downarrow}^{z}
for
z\in\{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{},\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{},\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}\}
,

and

, together with the four bipartitions
\downarrow^{1}
,
\downarrow^{0,2}\uparrow_{1}
,
\downarrow^{0,3}\uparrow_{1}
and
\downarrow^{2,3}\uparrow_{1}
. For example, the bipartition

above is
\operatorname{a}_{3}^{(1)}{}{\downarrow}^{2}

3.3
Inductive approach to the main theorem

Now we give some results to facilitate a proof of
1.1
by induction. We begin with an analogue of a result for partitions in
[
JM2
]
, which greatly restricts the set of bipartitions we need to consider. We give the result for blocks of weight
3
only, but a more general result along the lines of
[
JM2
, Proposition 2.1]
can easily be proved.

Lemma 3.1
.

Suppose
B
is a weight
3
block of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
, and that
1.1
holds with
n
replaced by any smaller integer. Suppose
\lambda,\mu
are bipartitions of
n
with
\mu
restricted, and
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
.

1.

If
\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)\geqslant\max\{1,\operatorname{rem}_{i}(\lambda)\}
, then
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]\leqslant 1
.

2.

If
\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)\geqslant\max\{1,\delta_{i}(B)+1\}
, then
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]\leqslant 1
.

Recall the notation
\epsilon_{i}M
from
Section

2.8
, and that (from
2.11
)
\epsilon_{i}\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}=\operatorname{rem}_{i}(\lambda)
and
\epsilon_{i}\operatorname{D}_{\mu}=\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)
.

1.

Since
\mathrm{e}_{i}
is an exact functor, if
M
is a module and
N
is a subquotient of
M
, then
\epsilon_{i}N\leqslant\epsilon_{i}M
. In particular, if
\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)>\operatorname{rem}_{i}(\lambda)
, then
\epsilon_{i}\operatorname{D}_{\mu}>\epsilon_{i}\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
, and therefore
\operatorname{D}_{\mu}
cannot be a composition factor of
\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}
.

Suppose instead that
\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)=\operatorname{rem}_{i}(\lambda)=r
, say. Then
r=\epsilon_{i}\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}=\epsilon_{i}\operatorname{D}_{\mu}
. Now
\mathrm{e}_{i}^{(r)}(\operatorname{S}_{\lambda})\cong\operatorname{S}_{\lambda^{-}}
, and
\mathrm{e}_{i}^{(r)}(\operatorname{D}_{\mu})\cong\operatorname{D}_{\mu^{-}}
, where
\lambda^{-}
is obtained by removing all the removable
i
-nodes from
\lambda
, and
\mu^{-}
is obtained by removing all the normal
i
-nodes from
\mu
. Therefore

[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda^{-}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu^{-}}]=[\mathrm{e}_{i}^{(r)}\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}:\operatorname{D}_{\mu^{-}}]=\sum_{\nu}[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\nu}][\mathrm{e}_{i}^{(r)}\operatorname{D}_{\nu}:\operatorname{D}_{\mu^{-}}]\geqslant[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}],

summing over restricted bipartitions
\nu
of
n
. Because
r=\operatorname{rem}_{i}(\lambda)
, we obtain
r\geqslant\delta_{i}(\lambda)
. So by
Lemma

2.5
the weight of
\lambda^{-}
is at most
3
. If
\lambda^{-}
has weight
3
, then by the inductive assumption
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda^{-}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu^{-}}]\leqslant 1
. If
\lambda^{-}
has weight less than
3
, then
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda^{-}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu^{-}}]\leqslant 1
from
2.6
. Either way, we obtain
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]\leqslant 1
.

2.

We show that the number
r=\operatorname{rem}_{i}(\lambda)
is at most
\max\{1,\delta_{i}(B)+1\}
; then in particular
r\leqslant\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)
, and we can use part (1) of the
Lemma
. Suppose for a contradiction that
r\geqslant 2
and
r\geqslant\delta_{i}(B)+2
, and let
\lambda^{-}
be obtained by removing all the removable
i
-nodes from
\lambda
. Then by
Lemma

2.5
the weight of
\lambda^{-}
equals
3-r(r-\delta_{i}(B))
. Since by assumption
r\geqslant 2
and
r-\delta_{i}(B)\geqslant 2
, this makes the weight of
\lambda^{-}
negative, a contradiction.∎

We deduce two very useful corollaries.

Corollary 3.2
.

Suppose
B
is a weight
3
block of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
with
\delta_{i}(B)\leqslant 0
for all
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
, and that
1.1
holds with
n
replaced by any smaller integer. Then
1.1
holds for
B
.

Suppose
\lambda,\mu
are bipartitions in
B
with
\mu
restricted. Then
\operatorname{D}_{\mu}\downarrow_{\mathcal{H}_{n-1}}\neq 0
, so
\mathrm{e}_{i}\operatorname{D}_{\mu}\neq 0
for some
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
. This means that
\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)\geqslant 1
, so
\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)\geqslant\max\{1,\delta_{i}(B)+1\}
, and therefore
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]\leqslant 1
by
Lemma

3.1
(2).
∎

Corollary 3.3
.

Suppose
B
is a weight
3
block of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
, and that
1.1
holds with
n
replaced by any smaller integer. If
\lambda
is a bipartition in
B
and
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
such that
\delta_{i}(B)\geqslant 1
and
\lambda
has no addable
i
-nodes, then
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]\leqslant 1
for all
\mu
.

The assumption that
\lambda
has no addable
i
-nodes means that
\operatorname{rem}_{i}(\lambda)=\delta_{i}(B)
, while
\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)\geqslant\delta_{i}(B)
. So
\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)\geqslant\max\{1,\operatorname{rem}_{i}(\lambda)\}
, and the result follows from
Lemma

3.1
(1).
∎

So to prove
1.1
by induction using
3.3
, it suffices to consider only those
\lambda
that have at least one addable
i
-node for
every

i
for which
\delta_{i}(B)\geqslant 1
. Call such
\lambda

exceptional
. The next few lemmas will show that in most cases
B
has no exceptional bipartitions.

Lemma 3.4
.

Suppose
B
is a core block, and that
\delta_{i}(B)\geqslant 1
for some
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
. Then
B
contains no exceptional bipartitions.

Suppose
\lambda
is a bipartition in
B
. Then we claim that
\lambda
has no addable
i
-nodes. Assume for a contradiction that
\lambda
has at least one addable
i
-node. Then because
\delta_{i}(B)\geqslant 1
, we know that
\lambda
has at least two removable
i
-nodes. The two components of
\lambda
are both
e
-cores, and an
e
-core cannot have addable and removable nodes of the same residue, so the addable
i
-nodes of
\lambda
are in one component and the removable
i
-nodes in the other. We assume that the removable
i
-nodes are in component
1
(the other case is similar). This means that in an abacus display for
\lambda
there are at least two positions
b
on runner
i
such that there is a bead in position
b
but not in position
b-1
. So there are at least two more beads on runner
i
than on runner
i-1
in component
1
(or at least three more, in the case
i=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}
). Similarly, in component
2
of the abacus display, there is at least one position
b
on runner
i-1
such that there is a bead at position
b
but no bead at position
b+1
. So there are more beads on runner
i-1
than on runner
i
in the component
2
(or at least as many beads on runner
i-1
as on runner
i
, in the case
i=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}
). We deduce that
\gamma_{i}(\lambda)-\gamma_{i-1}(\lambda)\geqslant 3
. But the assumption that
B
is a core block gives
\gamma_{i}(\lambda)-\gamma_{i-1}(\lambda)\leqslant 2
, a contradiction.
∎

In view of
Lemma

3.4
, it suffices to consider non-core blocks from now on.

Lemma 3.5
.

Suppose
\delta_{i}(B)\geqslant 3
for some
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
. Then
B
contains no exceptional bipartitions.

If
\lambda
is a bipartition in
B
, then we claim that
\lambda
cannot have an addable
i
-node: if it did, then by
Lemma

2.5
the weight of a bipartition obtained by adding an addable
i
-node to
\lambda
would be
3-(\delta_{i}(\lambda)+1)
, which is negative, a contradiction.
∎

Lemma 3.6
.

Suppose there are
i,j\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
such that
\delta_{i}(B),\delta_{j}(B)\geqslant 1
, and
j\neq i,i\pm 1
. Then
B
contains no exceptional bipartitions.

Suppose
\lambda
is an exceptional bipartition in
B
. Then
\lambda
has both an addable
i
-node
\mathfrak{m}
and an addable
j
-node
\mathfrak{n}
. Define bipartitions
\mu,\nu
by
[\mu]=[\lambda]\cup\{\mathfrak{m}\}
and
[\nu]=[\mu]\cup\{\mathfrak{n}\}
.
Lemma

2.5
then gives
\operatorname{wt}(\mu)=3-(\delta_{i}(B)+1)\leqslant 1
. Because
j\neq i,i\pm 1
, adding the
i
-node to
\lambda
does not affect the addable or removable
j
-nodes, so
\delta_{j}(\mu)=\delta_{j}(\lambda)
. Hence
\operatorname{wt}(\nu)=\operatorname{wt}(\mu)-(\delta_{j}(B)+1)\leqslant-1
, a contradiction.
∎

Lemma 3.7
.

Suppose there are
i,j\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
such that
i\neq j
,
\delta_{i}(B)\geqslant 1
and
\delta_{j}(B)\geqslant 2
. Then
B
contains no exceptional bipartitions.

If
j\neq i\pm 1
then the result follows from
Lemma

3.6
, so assume that
j=i+1
(the case
j=i-1
is similar). Suppose
\lambda
is an exceptional bipartition in
B
. Then
\lambda
has both an addable
i
-node
\mathfrak{m}
and an addable
(i+1)
-node
\mathfrak{n}
. Define bipartitions
\mu,\nu
by
[\mu]=[\lambda]\cup\{\mathfrak{m}\}
and
[\nu]=[\mu]\cup\{\mathfrak{n}\}
.
Lemma

2.5
now gives
\operatorname{wt}(\mu)=3-(\delta_{i}(B)+1)\leqslant 1
. Now from
[
F1
, Lemma 3.1]
we obtain
\delta_{i+1}(\mu)=\delta_{i+1}(\lambda)-1
, so that
\operatorname{wt}(\nu)=\operatorname{wt}(\mu)-\delta_{i+1}(B)\leqslant-1
, and again we have a contradiction.
∎

These lemmas mean that there are only four types of non-core block
B
in which there can be exceptional bipartitions. These are exactly analogous to the four types of weight
3
blocks of symmetric groups considered in
[
JM2
, Section 4]
. These types can be defined according to the values
\delta_{i}(B)
, as follows.

I.

\delta_{i}(B)\leqslant 0
for all
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
.

II.

There is
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
such that
\delta_{i}(B)=1
while
\delta_{j}(B)\leqslant 0
for all
j\neq i
.

III.

There is
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
such that
\delta_{i}(B)=\delta_{i+1}(B)=1
while
\delta_{j}(B)\leqslant 0
for all
j\neq i,i+1
.

IV.

There is
i\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
such that
\delta_{i}(B)=2
while
\delta_{j}(B)\leqslant 0
for all
j\neq i
.

We know from
3.2
that
1.1
holds for blocks of type I. To prove
1.1
, we need to show that if
B
is a block of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
of type II, III or IV and if
1.1
holds with
n
replaced by any smaller integer, then it holds for
B
. We address the three types of block in
Sections

4
,
5
and
6
.

4
Blocks of type II

Throughout this section, we assume
B
is a block of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
and
i\in\mathbb{Z}
is such that
\delta_{i}(B)=1
while
\delta_{j}(B)\leqslant 0
for all
j\not\equiv i\ (\operatorname{mod}\,e)
. Our aim is to show that if
1.1
holds with
n
replaced by any smaller integer, then it holds for
B
.

4.1
The abacus for a block of type II

Let
\xi
be the nucleus of
B
. Whenever we refer to the abacus display for
\xi
, we will mean the
(k_{1}+1,k_{2}-1)
-abacus display, and whenever we refer to the residues of nodes for
\xi
, we mean with respect to
(\kappa_{1}+1,\kappa_{2}-1)
. With this convention in mind, we have
\delta_{i}(\xi)=1
while
\delta_{j}(\xi)\leqslant 0
for
j\not\equiv i\ (\operatorname{mod}\,e)
. This means that
\xi
has exactly one removable node, which has residue
i
(because by
Lemma

2.5
a bipartition of weight
0
cannot have an addable and a removable node of the same residue). We will assume that this removable node lies in component
1
(in the opposite case we can replace
\kappa
with
(\kappa_{2},\kappa_{1})
and appeal to the results in
Section

2.7
).

By considering the abacus display for
\xi
and using the fact that
\xi
has
(\kappa_{1}+1,\kappa_{2}-1)
-weight
0
, we find that there are integers
i\leqslant j\leqslant k\leqslant l\leqslant e+i-2
such that in component
1
of
\xi
there is a removable
i
-node, and addable nodes of residues
j+1
and
l+1
, while in component
2
there is just an addable node of residue
k+1
(so in fact
\kappa_{1}=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{j}
, and
\kappa_{2}=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{k}
). We therefore have
Z=\{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{i},\dots,\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{j}\}\cup\{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{k},\dots,\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{l}\}
. The fact that
|Z|\geqslant 2
implies that either
i<j
or
k<l
.

.

e=11
,
\kappa=(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{},\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{})
and
\xi=\big(3^{3}\ \big|\ \varnothing\big)
, with the following abacus display.

, and

.

4.2
Exceptional bipartitions in
B

Suppose
\lambda
is a bipartition in
B
. From the results in
Section

3.3
, we need only consider Specht modules labelled by exceptional bipartitions; that is, those with addable
i
-nodes. By examining the abacus displays of the bipartitions in
B
, we can easily classify these. There are
3\lvert Z\rvert
exceptional bipartitions, which we label
\alpha_{x},\beta_{x},\gamma_{x}
for
x\in Z
as follows:

\alpha_{x}=\begin{cases}\operatorname{a}_{i}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{x}&\text{ if }x\neq i\\
\downarrow^{i-1}&\text{ if }x=i,\end{cases}\qquad\beta_{x}=\begin{cases}\operatorname{a}_{i-1}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{x}&\text{ if }x\neq i\\
\operatorname{a}_{i}^{(1)}{}{\downarrow}^{i}&\text{ if }x=i,\end{cases}\qquad\gamma_{x}=\begin{cases}\downarrow^{i,x}\uparrow_{i-1}&\text{ if }x\neq i\\
\operatorname{a}_{i-1}^{(1)}{}{\downarrow}^{i}&\text{ if }x=i.\end{cases}

It will be helpful to write these bipartitions explicitly:

\displaystyle\alpha_{x}

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\big((e+i-l)^{j-i+1},1^{l-i+1}\ \big|\ e+i-k-2\big)&\text{if }x=i\\
\hbox to350.0pt{$\big((e+i-l)^{j-x},(e+i-l-1)^{x-i}\ \big|\ e+x-k-1,e+i-k,1^{k-i}\big)$\hfil}&\text{if }i<x\leqslant j\\
\big((e+i-l)^{j-i+1},1^{l-x}\ \big|\ e+i-k-1,x-k,1^{k-i}\big)&\text{if }k<x\leqslant l,\end{cases}

\displaystyle\beta_{x}

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\big((e+i-l)^{j-i+1},1^{l-i}\ \big|\ e+i-k-1\big)&\text{if }x=i\\
\hbox to350.0pt{$\big((e+i-l)^{j-x},(e+i-l-1)^{x-i}\ \big|\ e+x-k-1,e+i-k-1,1^{k-i+1}\big)$\hfil}&\text{if }i<x\leqslant j\\
\big((e+i-l)^{j-i+1},1^{l-x}\ \big|\ e+i-k-2,x-k,1^{k-i+1}\big)&\text{if }k<x\leqslant l,\end{cases}

\displaystyle\gamma_{x}

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\big((e+i-l)^{j-i},e+i-l-1,1^{l-i+1}\ \big|\ e+i-k-1\big)&\text{if }x=i\\
\hbox to350.0pt{$\big((e+i-l)^{j-x},(e+i-l-1)^{x-i-1},e+i-l-2\ \big|\ e+x-k-1,e+i-k,1^{k-i+1}\big)$\hfil}&\text{if }i<x\leqslant j\\
\big((e+i-l)^{j-i},e+i-l-1,1^{l-x}\ \big|\ e+i-k-1,x-k,1^{k-i+1}\big)&\text{if }k<x\leqslant l.\end{cases}

Each exceptional bipartition has exactly one addable
i
-node, and the labelling is chosen so that
\alpha_{x},\beta_{x},\gamma_{x}
all yield the same bipartition when the addable
i
-node is added, with
\alpha_{x}\vartriangleright\beta_{x}\vartriangleright\gamma_{x}
.

4.3
Proving
1.1
in
B

Our aim is to show that
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]\leqslant 1
for all bipartitions
\lambda,\mu
in
B
, given the inductive assumption. We will do this by looking at one restricted bipartition
\mu
at a time. The next lemma will help in narrowing down the cases we need to consider.

Lemma 4.1
.

Suppose
\mu
is a restricted bipartition in
B
, and that
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]>1
for some
\lambda
. Then
\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)=1
, and there is some
x\in Z
for which
[\operatorname{S}_{\alpha_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
,
[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
,
[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
are all non-zero; in particular,
\mu^{\diamond}\trianglerighteqslant\alpha_{x},\beta_{x},\gamma_{x}\trianglerighteqslant\mu
.

If
\lambda
is such that
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]>1
, then
\lambda
is exceptional, so
\lambda\in\{\alpha_{x},\beta_{x},\gamma_{x}\}
for some
x
. The conclusion that
\mu
has only one normal node comes from
Lemma

3.1
(2).

Now we claim that
[\operatorname{S}_{\alpha_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}],[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}],[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]\geqslant 1
, which gives the result using
2.13
. Each of
\alpha_{x},\beta_{x},\gamma_{x}
has two removable
i
-nodes, and the branching rules show that there are bipartitions
\hat{\alpha}_{x},\hat{\beta}_{x},\hat{\gamma}_{x}
of
n-1
such that

\displaystyle\mathrm{e}_{i}\operatorname{S}_{\alpha_{x}}

\displaystyle\sim\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\alpha}_{x}}+\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{x}},

\displaystyle\mathrm{e}_{i}\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{x}}

\displaystyle\sim\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\alpha}_{x}}+\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\gamma}_{x}},

\displaystyle\mathrm{e}_{i}\operatorname{S}_{\gamma_{x}}

\displaystyle\sim\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{x}}+\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\gamma}_{x}}.

Because
\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)=1
, there is a restricted bipartition
\tilde{\mu}
such that
\mathrm{e}_{i}\operatorname{D}_{\mu}\cong\operatorname{D}_{\tilde{\mu}}
. Now (analogously to the proof of
[
F4
, Proposition 2.8(2)]
) we obtain

[\operatorname{S}_{\alpha_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]+[\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\gamma}_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\tilde{\mu}}]=[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]+[\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\tilde{\mu}}]=[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]+[\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\alpha}_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\tilde{\mu}}].

Since by assumption the decomposition numbers for weight
3
blocks of
\mathcal{H}_{n-1}
are all
0
or
1
, this means that the decomposition numbers
[\operatorname{S}_{\alpha_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
,
[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
,
[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
differ by at most
1
. So if one of them is greater than
1
, then they are all positive.
∎

Lemma

4.1
greatly restricts the set of restricted bipartitions
\mu
that we need to consider. To apply
Lemma

4.1
we look at the Jantzen–Schaper dominance order among the exceptional bipartitions, which is easy to check given the explicit description above: if
\epsilon
is any of the symbols
\alpha,\beta,\gamma
, then

\epsilon_{i}\vartriangleright\epsilon_{k+1}\vartriangleright\epsilon_{k+2}\vartriangleright\cdots\vartriangleright\epsilon_{l}\vartriangleright\epsilon_{i+1}\vartriangleright\epsilon_{i+2}\vartriangleright\cdots\vartriangleright\epsilon_{j}.

In particular, the most dominant
\gamma_{x}
is
\gamma_{i}
. So to show that
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]\leqslant 1
for all
\mu
, we need only consider bipartitions
\mu
for which:

1.

\mu
is restricted;

2.

\gamma_{i}\trianglerighteqslant\mu
; and

3.

\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)=1
, and
\operatorname{nor}_{j}(\mu)=0
for all
j\neq i
.

Analysis of the possible abacus configurations enables a classification of the bipartitions
\mu
satisfying (
2
) and (
3
). By working through the different bipartitions in
B
, we can check that the only bipartitions
\mu
satisfying these conditions are
\operatorname{a}_{i-1}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i}
and
\operatorname{a}_{i}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i}
.

(Note that if
i<k
then the bipartition
\mu=\operatorname{a}_{k}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i}
does not satisfy (
2
): in this case

\displaystyle\mu

\displaystyle=\big((e+i-l)^{j-i}\ \big|\ e-1,e+i-k\big),

\displaystyle\gamma_{i}

\displaystyle=\big((e+i-l)^{j-i},e+i-l-1,1^{l-i+1}\ \big|\ e+i-k-1\big),

so
\gamma_{i}\vartriangleright\mu
in the usual dominance order. But by examining residues we can check that
\gamma_{i}\not\vartriangleright\mu
in the Jantzen–Schaper dominance order.)

Now we introduce condition (1). First, from
Lemma

2.1
we know that
\operatorname{a}_{i}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i}
is not restricted, since its second component is not
e
-restricted. So it remains to check when
\mu=\operatorname{a}_{i-1}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i}
is restricted. We do this by removing good nodes, using the results of
Section

2.4
.

We begin by drawing an abacus display for
\mu
(where we adjust the numbers of beads in order to make runner
i-1
the leftmost runner).

This bipartition lies in the weight
1
block underlying
B
, and (from the results in
Section

2.4
) is restricted if and only if
\mu
is. Hence we need to understand whether
\xi
is restricted or not.
[
F1
, Lemma 4.9]
shows that a bipartition of weight
1
is restricted if and only if it is not the most dominant bipartition in its block. Using the explicit description of weight 1 blocks
[
F1
, Theorem 4.4]
, we find all the bipartitions in the same block as
\xi
and we see that
\xi
is the most dominant bipartition in its block if and only if
k=l
. It follows that
\mu
is restricted if and only if
k<l
.

We deal with this case using the Jantzen–Schaper formula. From
Lemma

4.1
we need only consider exceptional bipartitions
\alpha_{x},\beta_{x},\gamma_{x}
for which
\gamma_{x}\trianglerighteqslant\mu
, and by looking at the explicit expressions for the exceptional bipartitions, we find that this happens if and only if
x=i
or
k<x\leqslant l
. So to show that
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]\leqslant 1
for all
\lambda
it suffices to show that

[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma_{i}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma_{k+1}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=\dots=[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma_{l-1}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{l}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=0.

To do this using the Jantzen–Schaper order, we first find all the bipartitions
\lambda
such that
\beta_{l}\trianglerighteqslant\lambda\trianglerighteqslant\mu
or
\gamma_{x}\trianglerighteqslant\lambda\trianglerighteqslant\mu
for some
x\in\{i\}\cup\{k+1,\dots,l\}
. In fact by examining the explicit forms of these bipartitions, we easily find that the only such bipartitions
\lambda
are
\mu
,
\beta_{l}
,
\gamma_{i}
and
\gamma_{k+1},\dots,\gamma_{l}
, with the Jantzen–Schaper order on these bipartitions given by the following diagram.

\mu
\gamma_{l}
\beta_{l}
\gamma_{k+1}
\gamma_{i}

The Jantzen–Schaper coefficients we need are given by

j_{\mu\gamma_{x}}=\begin{cases}(-1)^{l-x}&(k<x\leqslant l)\\
(-1)^{l-k}&(x=i),\end{cases}\qquad j_{\mu\beta_{l}}=-1,\qquad j_{\gamma_{l}\gamma_{x}}=\begin{cases}(-1)^{l-x+1}&(k<x<l)\\
(-1)^{l-k+1}&(x=i),\end{cases}\qquad j_{\gamma_{l}\beta_{l}}=1.

Now we deduce that
[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma_{l}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=1
, and then (successively)
[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma_{l-1}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=\dots=[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma_{k+1}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma_{i}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=0
as well as
[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{l}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=0
.

5
Blocks of type III

Throughout this section, we assume
B
is a block of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
and
i\in\mathbb{Z}
is such that
\delta_{i}(B)=\delta_{i+1}(B)=1
while
\delta_{j}(B)\leqslant 0
for all
j\not\equiv i,i+1\ (\operatorname{mod}\,e)
. Our aim is to show that if
1.1
holds with
n
replaced by any smaller integer, then it holds for
B
.

5.1
The abacus for a block of type III

Let
\xi
be the nucleus of
B
. Whenever we refer to the abacus display for
\xi
, we will mean the
(k_{1}+1,k_{2}-1)
-abacus display, and whenever we refer to the residues of nodes for
\xi
, we mean with respect to
(\kappa_{1}+1,\kappa_{2}-1)
. With this convention in mind, we have
\delta_{i}(\xi)=\delta_{i+1}(\xi)=1
while
\delta_{j}(\xi)\leqslant 0
for
j\not\equiv i,i+1\ (\operatorname{mod}\,e)
. This means that
\xi
has exactly two removable nodes, of residues
i
and
i+1
. We will assume that the removable
(i+1)
-node lies in component
1
(in the opposite case we can replace
\kappa
with
(\kappa_{2},\kappa_{1})
and appeal to the results in
Section

2.7
). This means in particular that
\gamma_{i+1}(\xi)=\gamma_{i}(\xi)+1
. Now we claim that the removable
i
-node of
\xi
must lie in component
2
; if not, then we obtain
\gamma_{i}(\xi)=\gamma_{i-1}(\xi)+1
and hence
\gamma_{i+1}(\xi)-\gamma_{i-1}(\xi)=2
, and now the results in
Section

3.1
show that
\xi
has positive weight, a contradiction.

Now we can describe the abacus display for
\xi
more precisely: there are integers
i+1\leqslant j\leqslant k\leqslant l\leqslant m\leqslant e+i-2
such that in component
1
of
\xi
there is a removable node of residue
i+1
and addable nodes of residues
j+1
and
l+1
, while in component
2
there is a removable node of residue
i
and addable nodes of residues
k+1
and
m+1
. (So in fact
\kappa_{1}=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{j}
, and
\kappa_{2}=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{k}
). We therefore have
Z=\{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{i},\dots,\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{j}\}\cup\{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{k},\dots,\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{l}\}\cup\{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{m},\dots,\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{i}\}
.

e=14
,
\kappa=(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{},\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{})
and
\xi=\big(7^{2}\ \big|\ 3^{6}\big)
, with the following abacus display.
