Observe that
\alpha\beta\vartriangleright\alpha\gamma,\gamma\alpha\vartriangleright\beta\gamma
(and in fact
\alpha\gamma
and
\gamma\alpha
are incomparable even in the usual dominance order).

5.3
Proving
1.1
in
B

Now we consider what conditions we need on a restricted bipartition
\mu
in order to have
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]>1
for some
\lambda
.

Lemma 5.1
.

Suppose
\mu
is a restricted bipartition in
B
, and
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]>1
for some
\lambda
. Then
\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)=\operatorname{nor}_{i+1}(\mu)=1
, and at least three of the decomposition numbers
[\operatorname{S}_{\alpha\beta}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
,
[\operatorname{S}_{\alpha\gamma}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
,
[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma\alpha}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
and
[\operatorname{S}_{\beta\gamma}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
are positive. Hence
\mu^{\diamond}\trianglerighteqslant\alpha\gamma,\gamma\alpha\trianglerighteqslant\mu
.

In the same way as in the proof of
Lemma

4.1
, we can apply the restriction functor
\mathrm{e}_{i}
to show that
\mu
has only one normal
i
-node and that if either of the decomposition numbers
[\operatorname{S}_{\alpha\beta}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
and
[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma\alpha}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
is greater than
1
then they are both positive, while if either of
[\operatorname{S}_{\alpha\gamma}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
and
[\operatorname{S}_{\beta\gamma}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
is greater than
1
then they are both positive. But in the same way we can use
\mathrm{e}_{i+1}
to show that
\operatorname{nor}_{i+1}(\mu)=1
and either
[\operatorname{S}_{\alpha\beta}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
and
[\operatorname{S}_{\alpha\gamma}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
are both positive or
[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma\alpha}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
and
[\operatorname{S}_{\beta\gamma}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
are both positive. Combining these statements shows that at least three of the given decomposition numbers are positive. Now
2.13
, together with the Jantzen–Schaper dominance order on the bipartitions
\alpha\beta,\alpha\gamma,\gamma\alpha,\beta\gamma
gives the second statement.
∎

So to prove our main result for
B
we can focus on bipartitions
\mu
in
B
for which:

1.

\mu
is restricted;

2.

\alpha\gamma,\gamma\alpha\trianglerighteqslant\mu
;

3.

\mu^{\diamond}\trianglerighteqslant\alpha\gamma,\gamma\alpha
; and

4.

\operatorname{nor}_{i}(\mu)=\operatorname{nor}_{i+1}(\mu)=1
, and
\operatorname{nor}_{j}(\mu)=0
for
j\neq i,i+1
.

We begin by finding the bipartitions
\mu
for which conditions (
2
) and (
4
) are satisfied. A careful analysis of the possible abacus configurations shows that this happens in the cases given in the following table.

\mu

conditions

\operatorname{a}_{m}^{(1)}{}{\downarrow}^{i+1}

l<m

\operatorname{a}_{i-1}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i+1}

-

\operatorname{a}_{i}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i+1}

-

\operatorname{a}_{l}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i+1}

k<l=m

\operatorname{a}_{m}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i+1}

l<m

\downarrow^{i+1,i+2}\uparrow_{m}

i+1<j,\ l<m

\downarrow^{i+1,k+1}\uparrow_{m}

k<l<m

(Note in particular that the bipartitions
\mu=\operatorname{a}_{i+1}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i+1}
and
\operatorname{a}_{k}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i+1}
(with
i+1<k
) do not appear; these bipartitions satisfy (
2
) and (
4
) if the usual dominance order is used, but
\alpha\gamma\ntrianglerighteqslant\mu
in the Jantzen–Schaper dominance order.)

We next want to check which of these bipartitions are restricted. To do this we use (and extend) the technique that we used for the bipartition
\operatorname{a}_{i-1}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i}
in
Section

4.3
. Given a bipartition
\mu
in the above table, we repeatedly remove good nodes until we reach a bipartition
\xi
which has weight
0
or
1
, or has no normal nodes. If
\xi
has no normal nodes (but is not the empty bipartition) then
\xi
is not restricted, and so neither is
\mu
. If
\xi
has weight
0
then it is restricted; if
\xi
has weight
1
, then it is restricted if and only if it is not the most dominant bipartition in its block.

If we determine that
\mu
is restricted via this technique, we can also use it to construct
\mu^{\diamond}
. Suppose we have reached the restricted bipartition
\xi
of weight
0
or
1
by removing good nodes of residues
r_{1},\dots,r_{t}
in turn. The bipartition
\xi^{\diamond}
can easily be identified: if
\xi
has weight
0
then
\xi^{\diamond}=\xi
, while if
\xi
has weight
1
then (from
[
F1
, Lemma 4.9]
)
\xi^{\diamond}
is the minimal bipartition in the same block as
\xi
for which
\xi^{\diamond}\vartriangleright\xi
. Having identified
\xi^{\diamond}
, we add anticogood nodes of residues
r_{t},\dots,r_{1}
in turn, and by
2.9
we obtain
\mu^{\diamond}
.

.

and let

, with the following abacus display. (We modify the abacus display by adjusting the numbers of beads in order to make runner
i-1
the leftmost runner).

Assume
k=l
and let
\mu=\operatorname{a}_{i}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i+1}
. In this case we will show that
[\operatorname{S}_{\alpha\gamma}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=[\operatorname{S}_{\gamma\alpha}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=0

[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]\leqslant 1
for all
\lambda
by

5.1
. To do this, we use the Jantzen–Schaper formula. First we find all bipartitions in the set

D=\left\{\left.\lambda\ \right|\ \smash{\text{$\lambda\trianglerighteqslant\mu$ and either $\alpha\gamma\trianglerighteqslant\lambda$ or $\gamma\alpha\trianglerighteqslant\lambda$}}\right\}.

By examining abacus displays, we find that

\displaystyle D={}

\displaystyle\left\{\left.\operatorname{a}_{x}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i+1}\ \right|\ \smash{i\leqslant x\leqslant k}\right\}\cup\left\{\left.\downarrow^{x}\ \right|\ \smash{j+1\leqslant x\leqslant k}\right\}

\displaystyle\cup\left\{\left.\operatorname{a}_{x}^{(1)}{}{\downarrow}^{x}\ \right|\ \smash{i+1\leqslant x\leqslant j}\right\}\cup\{\beta\gamma,\alpha\gamma,\gamma\alpha\}.

, then

Now the fact that

Case

\displaystyle=k_{1}+k_{2}+e-l,

\displaystyle l^{\prime}

\displaystyle=k_{1}+k_{2}+e-k,

\displaystyle m^{\prime}

\displaystyle=k_{1}+k_{2}+e-j.

In the block
B^{\prime}
,
(\mu^{\diamond})^{\prime}
is the bipartition
\operatorname{a}_{i^{\prime}}^{(2)}{}{\downarrow}^{i^{\prime}+1}
, with
j^{\prime}=k^{\prime}=l^{\prime}
. So using case
dealt with above, we can deduce that
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{(\mu^{\diamond})^{\prime}}]\leqslant 1
for all
\lambda
, and therefore (by
2.7
)
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]\leqslant 1
for all
\lambda
.

5.6
Case
2

In this case we use a conjugation argument, as we did for case
above. In this case
(\mu^{\diamond})^{\prime}
satisfies the conditions of case
above, therefore we can deduce that
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]\leqslant 1
for all
\lambda
in the same way.

This deals with all cases, and so our inductive step for type III blocks is complete.

6
Blocks of type IV

The last situation we have to investigate is when
B
is a block of
\mathcal{H}_{n}
and
i\in\mathbb{Z}
is such that
\delta_{i}(B)=2
and
\delta_{j}(B)\leqslant 0
for every
j\not\equiv i\ (\operatorname{mod}\,e)
. Again we will follow an inductive approach to show that
1.1
holds for
B
.

6.1
The abacus for a block of type IV

Take
\xi
the nucleus of
B
and consider its
(k_{1}+1,k_{2}-1)
-abacus display following the same convention of
Sections

4
and
5
. Then
\gamma_{i}(\xi)=2
and
\gamma_{j}(\xi)\leqslant 0
for every
j\not\equiv i\ (\operatorname{mod}\,e)
and we note that
\xi
has exactly two removable
i
-nodes (again because
\xi
has weight 0 and by
Lemma

2.5
it cannot have both removable and addable nodes of the same residue). We now observe that these two removable nodes occur in different components of
\xi
. Assuming the contrary we would have that
\gamma_{i}(\xi)-\gamma_{i-1}(\xi)=2
but
\xi
has weight 0 and
{\gamma_{x}(\xi)-\gamma_{y}(\xi)}\leqslant 1
for every
x,y\in\mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}
.

Similarly to the previous sections we draw the
(k_{1}+1,k_{2}-1)
-abacus display of
\xi
finding integers
i\leqslant j\leqslant k\leqslant l\leqslant m\leqslant e+i-2
such that
\xi
has a removable
i
-node in both components and addable nodes of residue
j+1
and
l+1
in component 1 and of residue
k+1
and
m+1
in component 2 (in particular
\kappa_{1}=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{j}
, and
\kappa_{2}=\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{k}
). Now
Z=\{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{i},\dots,\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{j}\}\cup\{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{k},\dots,\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{l}\}\cup\{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{m},\dots,\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{i}\}
.

.

e=17
,
\kappa=(\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{},\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{})
and
\xi=\big(7^{4}\ \big|\ 4^{7}\big)
, with the following abacus display.

In contrast to Case III, these bipartitions are totally ordered by the Jantzen–Schaper dominance order; in particular
\beta_{4}\vartriangleright\beta_{3}\vartriangleright\beta_{2}\vartriangleright\beta_{1}
.

6.3
Proving
1.1
in
B

Also in this situation it is useful to establish a lemma that brings out a useful property of those restricted bipartitions
\mu
such that
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]>1
for some
\lambda
. By
Lemma

3.1
(2) we note that such bipartitions have exactly two normal
i
-nodes.

Lemma 6.1
.

Suppose
\mu
is a restricted bipartition in
B
, and
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]>1
for some
\lambda
. Then the decomposition numbers
[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{1}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}],[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{2}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}],[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{3}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}],[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{4}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]

are all positive; in particular
\mu^{\diamond}\trianglerighteqslant\beta_{4}\vartriangleright\beta_{3}\vartriangleright\beta_{2}\vartriangleright\beta_{1}\trianglerighteqslant\mu
.

Let
\lambda
be a bipartition such that
[\operatorname{S}_{\lambda}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]>1
. Then
\lambda=\beta_{x}
for some
x\in\{1,2,3,4\}
. We follow the same idea as in
Lemmas

4.1
and
5.1
with the only difference that here we need to apply the restriction functor
\mathrm{e}_{i}
to
\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{1}},\dots,\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{4}}
’twice’, namely we apply the functor
\mathrm{e}_{i}^{2}
described in
Section

2.8
. By the branching rules we find that there are bipartitions
\hat{\beta}_{1},\hat{\beta}_{2},\hat{\beta}_{3},\hat{\beta}_{4},\tilde{\mu}
of
n-2
such that

\displaystyle\mathrm{e}_{i}^{2}\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{1}}

\displaystyle\sim(\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{1}})^{2}+(\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{2}})^{2}+(\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{3}})^{2},

\displaystyle\mathrm{e}_{i}^{2}\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{2}}

\displaystyle\sim(\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{1}})^{2}+(\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{2}})^{2}+(\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{4}})^{2},

\displaystyle\mathrm{e}_{i}^{2}\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{3}}

\displaystyle\sim(\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{1}})^{2}+(\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{3}})^{2}+(\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{4}})^{2},

\displaystyle\mathrm{e}_{i}^{2}\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{4}}

\displaystyle\sim(\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{2}})^{2}+(\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{3}})^{2}+(\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{4}})^{2},

\displaystyle\mathrm{e}_{i}^{2}\operatorname{D}_{\mu}

\displaystyle\sim\operatorname{D}_{\tilde{\mu}}.

Analogously as in
[
F4
, Proposition 2.10(4)]
, we find

[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{1}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]+[\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{4}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\tilde{\mu}}]=[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{2}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]+[\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{3}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\tilde{\mu}}]=[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{3}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]+[\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{2}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\tilde{\mu}}]=[\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{4}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]+[\operatorname{S}_{\hat{\beta}_{1}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\tilde{\mu}}].

and we conclude by induction that if one of the decomposition numbers
[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{x}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]
is greater than
1
, then they are all positive. The last sentence follows from
2.13
.
∎

and two simple modules labelled by
\mu
and
\beta_{1}
. It is easy to solve this case by hand. We use a dimension argument here. First we note that the two Specht modules
\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{1}}
and
\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{2}}
have the same dimension. From our calculations above we know that

[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{1}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=1,

while
2.13
and a very simple calculation with the Jantzen–Schaper formula show that

[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{1}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\beta_{1}}]=[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{2}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\beta_{1}}]=1,

forcing
[\operatorname{S}_{\beta_{2}}\nolinebreak:\nolinebreak\operatorname{D}_{\mu}]=1
.

This completes the proof of Case IV, and of our main theorem.
